newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: Guterres sees Amsterdam EMU deal "in principle".
newsitem.headline: Guterres sees Amsterdam EMU deal "in principle".

text.p: Portugal's Prime Minister Antonio Guterres said on Monday that European Union leaders could reach agreement in principle during their Amsterdam summit on how to move forward on monetary union, even if it was unlikely that a formal deal would be signed.
"I think it will be possible to reach an agreement in principle," he told TSF radio from Amsterdam, where he is attending the two-day meeting of the 15-nation bloc.

Guterres was referring to the contentious issue of the stability pact, an accord on future budgetary discipline which France's recently-elected Socialist-led government wants extended to include commitments to fight unemployment.
The Portuguese Socialist leader, who backs the French government stand over unemployment, said that it was possible that "nothing will be signed" in Amsterdam.
But this should not stop European leaders reaching a political accord on a compromise, the details of which could be settled later, he said.
"I am not worried about signatures...my concern is that we make progress towards an indispensable accord to give tranquillity to (financial) markets," he said.
Guterres said such an accord would involve the stability pact being widened to bring in a commitment to battle unemployment within the European Union, where some 18 million people are without work.
He said that EU leaders needed to send out a clear message that the single currency was an irreversible project and that the January 1, 1999, date for its launch would be met.

In an interview with the Publico newspaper on Monday, Guterres said that the Maastricht Treaty was sufficiently flexible to let countries join the single currency even if their budget deficits were slightly above the indicated ceiling of three percent of gross domestic product (GDP).
Not just Italy but also France and Germany could face problems in complying with a rigid three percent limit for 1997, the year in which economic and monetary union (EMU) criteria should be met.

But he said that even if these countries had deficits of 3.2 percent of GDP in 1997 -- as predicted by the Paris-based Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) -- this should not prevent them joining at the start.
Guterres said any delay to the launch of monetary union would be extremely grave and could even mean that it would never be achieved.

Portugal, which has set qualifying for monetary union as its top policy priority, is on target to meet the key tests for entry -- the budget deficit and inflation -- and is tipped by many analysts to join EMU from its launch.
